source.version: arXiv:2604.13956v1, 15 April 2026; full text including Appendices A-E
source.title_on_document: Creo: From One-Shot Image Generation to Progressive, Co-Creative Ideation

supplement.holds: Illustrative workflows and system diagrams; participant screening, counterbalancing sequences, session protocol, annotation scheme, and metric definitions in Appendix D (pp. 14-17). Appendix D.7 describes the image metric as cosine similarity, whereas Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1 describe L2 distance. No additional inferential statistics for the image-distance contrast are reported.

paper_design_summary: A remotely moderated, counterbalanced within-participant study had 15 participants use Creo and a prompt-centric ChatGPT image interface to design their ideal living room and kitchen, using a different tool for each prompt (p. 7, Section 4.1). Tool and prompt orders were counterbalanced, but allocation to sequences and randomization were not stated (p. 15, Appendix D.2 and Table 2). The study compared first-to-final image embedding distances within sessions, interaction metrics, and qualitative reflections; Figure 4 additionally describes less clustering across participants without a numerical between-person diversity contrast (pp. 7-8, Sections 4.2-4.3.1 and Figure 4).

studies.label: One-shot versus progressive image-generation user study

assignment.what_was_assigned: Tool order (Creo versus ChatGPT baseline) and prompt order (ideal living room versus ideal kitchen). Each participant used both tools, one per prompt. Four counterbalancing sequences are listed, but the mechanism for allocating participants to sequences is not stated; counterbalancing alone does not establish random assignment.
assignment.quote: Each participant completed both prompts, using one prompt per tool. Tool order and prompt order were counterbalanced across participants using four sequences (Table 2).
assignment.locator: p. 15, Appendix D.2, Study Design, and Table 2; p. 7, Section 4.1, Study Overview.

arms.name: Progressive Staging (Creo)
arms.description: Staged image generation with editable intermediate representations, direct manipulation, AI-assisted edits, and preservation of prior decisions. The same participants also completed the baseline condition (p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Figure 4).

arms.name: One-Shot Baseline (ChatGPT/GPT)
arms.description: Multi-turn prompt-centric text-to-image interface supporting prompt refinement, regeneration, and masked edits. The same participants also completed Creo (p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Figure 4).

participants.who: Participants with visual-design experience recruited through Reddit and university communities focused on illustration, art, and design. The sample includes creative practitioners, and Appendix C identifies an architecture student from the user study. The reported sample is 15 people; Figure 4 displays participants P1-P15 under both conditions, so the arm counts refer to the same people. A separate analyzed-sample flow count is not stated.
participants.quote: We recruited 15 participants through posts in online (Reddit) and university communities focused on illustration, art, and design.
participants.locator: p. 7, Sections 4.1 and 4.1.1 (sample and completion of both conditions); p. 8, Figure 4 (P1-P15 in both conditions); p. 13, Appendix C (architecture student).

ai_tool.name_model: Creo (underlying image-generation model not stated); ChatGPT baseline (model/version not stated).
ai_tool.how_used: Creo exposes viewpoint, composition, color, lighting, and style through editable intermediate images; users can draw, mask, make AI-assisted changes, revisit stages, and preserve previous decisions. The baseline supports iterative text prompts, image regeneration, and masked edits (pp. 3-7, Sections 3 and 4.1).

task.description: Generate an image of an ideal living room and an image of an ideal kitchen, completing one prompt with each tool; tool and prompt orders were counterbalanced. Participants thought aloud while working (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.1.2; p. 15, Appendices D.2-D.4).
task.duration: Approximately 14 minutes per condition within an approximately 60-minute remotely moderated session (p. 7, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2; p. 15, Appendix D.3).

outcomes.name: Anchoring: first-to-final image embedding distance within a participant session
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: L2 distance between first and last generated images in CLIP space: Creo M = 0.75, SD = 0.13; GPT M = 0.46, SD = 0.31. The main text interprets larger distance as weaker anchoring. Each comparison is between images from the same participant session, not between different people. Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1 describe L2 distance between unit-normalized CLIP embeddings, but Appendix D.7 describes cosine similarity using OpenCLIP with L2-normalized embeddings; this inconsistency is unresolved. No inferential test for this contrast is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.3.1 and Figure 4 (means and SDs); p. 7, Section 4.2, RQ1 (L2-distance definition); p. 16, Appendix D.7 (cosine-similarity definition and session-level aggregation).

outcomes.name: Across-participant clustering of image embeddings (qualitative Figure 4 claim)
outcomes.question: across_people

contrasts.reported: The Figure 4 caption describes Creo image embeddings as less tightly clustered than GPT embeddings. The figure plots first and last images across participants, but no numerical contrast or inferential test of between-person diversity is reported. The numerical distances reported in Section 4.3.1 instead compare first and final images within participant sessions.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Figure 4, especially the embedding scatterplot and caption; Section 4.3.1.

diversity_detail.metric: Qualitative visual comparison of clustering in the CLIP embedding scatterplot; axes labeled PC1 and PC2. No numerical between-person diversity statistic is reported (p. 8, Figure 4).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: CLIP in the main text (pp. 7-8, Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1); Appendix D.7 names OpenCLIP for the first-to-final analysis (p. 16). The exact embedding checkpoint and the projection procedure for Figure 4 are not stated.
diversity_detail.computed_over: First and final generated images across participants within each tool condition (Creo and GPT), shown in the embedding scatterplot (p. 8, Figure 4).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical between-person diversity contrast, standard error, confidence interval, or inferential test is reported; the evidence is a qualitative visual comparison (p. 8, Figure 4 and Section 4.3.1; p. 16, Appendix D.7).
diversity_detail.notes: The caption describes Creo embeddings as less tightly clustered, coded as greater diversity. The numerical first-to-final summaries compare images within participant sessions and are not estimates of between-person diversity. Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1 define L2 distance between unit-norm CLIP embeddings (pp. 7-8), whereas Appendix D.7 defines cosine similarity using OpenCLIP with L2-normalized embeddings (p. 16); this inconsistency is unresolved.

eligibility.reason: The study has 15 unique analyzed participants, below the 50-person threshold; both conditions use the same people (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.1.1; p. 8, Figure 4). Tool and prompt orders were counterbalanced using listed sequences, but random assignment or another sequence-allocation mechanism is not stated (p. 15, Appendix D.2 and Table 2). Design is therefore coded other rather than assuming either random or non-random allocation. An output-based embedding score is reported, so criterion 3 is met, but it measures within-session anchoring; the across-person homogeneity claim has only a visual comparison and no numerical diversity contrast (pp. 7-8, Sections 4.2-4.3.1 and Figure 4; p. 16, Appendix D.7). This small comparison is excluded from core and is not classified as established observational context.

one_line_finding: In 15 participants, Creo had greater first-to-final within-session CLIP L2 distance than ChatGPT (M = 0.75, SD = 0.13 versus M = 0.46, SD = 0.31), interpreted as weaker anchoring; random assignment was not stated, and these numbers do not measure diversity across people (p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 4.3.1 and Figure 4; p. 15, Appendix D.2).
